paragraphs: Friend, this one is heavy, so let's say it plain. The LORD says, "I have forsaken My house; I have abandoned My inheritance" (Jeremiah 12:7). He calls His people "the beloved of My soul," and she has "roared against Me" (Jeremiah 12:8). The lesson is that the LORD takes His people's turning from Him seriously, and so should we.

But the passage doesn't end in the wreckage. Sown wheat, harvested thorns, and the LORD says they must bear the shame of that harvest (Jeremiah 12:13). Then comes the turn: after the uprooting, "I will once again have compassion on them and return each one to his inheritance and to his land" (Jeremiah 12:15). I know a little about being yanked out and set down somewhere dark, and I can tell you that being uprooted was never the last word for me either. The last word is compassion.

And that door isn't only open to the people of Judah. Even the evil neighbors get an if: if they learn His ways and swear by His name, "then they will be established among My people" (Jeremiah 12:16). But if they will not obey, the LORD says He will uproot that nation (Jeremiah 12:17). So here's the big idea, baker: the LORD means what He says, His compassion is real, and the way to stand in His house is to listen and obey.
